nutshell: In Lifelong Person Re-ID (L-ReID), updating the model on new data normally requires 're-indexing' - recomputing features for every old gallery image with the new model - but this is impossible when old raw images can't be kept for privacy reasons, leaving stale old-model gallery features incompatible with new-model query features. The paper formalizes this as Re-indexing Free Lifelong ReID (RFL-ReID) and proposes C2R, which instead continuously transforms the old gallery feature vectors themselves (never the raw images) into the current feature space via a cascaded transfer network plus two distillation modules that balance compatibility with anti-forgetting.
contributions: Formalizes RFL-ReID as a distinct, more realistic evaluation setting than standard L-ReID - raw gallery images from earlier stages are permanently inaccessible, only their previously-computed feature vectors persist - and quantifies how much existing L-ReID methods degrade under this constraint (Fig. 2: up to -17.6 R@1 / -9.3 mAP versus the same methods when re-indexing is allowed).

A Continual Compatible Transfer (CCT) network: 4 cascaded two-stream modules that update an old-stage gallery feature into the current feature space, combining a prototype-based 'knowledge capturing' branch (projecting onto learnable new-domain prototypes) with a direct forward-mapping MLP branch (preserving old-domain information), fused via a per-sample learned gating factor plus a residual connection.

Balanced Compatible Distillation (BCD): aligns transferred features to the new feature space both directly (L2 loss) and via a relationship-preserving KL-divergence term over a similarity matrix with same-identity pairs excluded, to avoid the direct-alignment term conflicting with relationship preservation.

Balanced Anti-forgetting Distillation (BAD): uses the old model's frozen classifier to distill old-class discriminability into the transferred features, plus a discriminative-consistency loss keeping transferred and newly-extracted features moving in a consistent direction relative to the original old feature.

Reports state-of-the-art average performance on both the new RFL-ReID setting and the traditional (re-indexing-allowed) L-ReID setting from a single trained model, across two dataset orderings and five benchmarks, with the lowest measured 'Average Forgetting' among all compared methods.
deficiencies: Evaluation uses a non-standard protocol inherited from prior work: each dataset is randomly subsampled to 500 identities (not the standard full test set), and CUHK-SYSU uses ground-truth-box cropping rather than its usual detection-based evaluation - the reported mAP/R@1 numbers therefore aren't directly comparable to the broader (non-lifelong) ReID literature's usual numbers on Market-1501/DukeMTMC/etc., even though the standard dataset papers are cited as the source.

On the traditional L-ReID task (Table 1, Order-1), the method does not actually win on every dataset despite leading on average: PatchKD beats it outright on DukeMTMC-ReID on both mAP and R@1, and on CUHK03 the method wins mAP but loses R@1 - the 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on the averaged metric, not universal per-dataset superiority.

The ablation on the CCT network's own headline mechanism - the adaptively-learned per-sample balancing factor a^m (Table 4) - shows it beats the best fixed constant value by a fairly small margin (39.5 mAP vs. 39.0 for a fixed 0.4), with most fixed values in the 0.2-1.0 range already landing within about 1 point of the adaptive version, so the specific 'adaptive' contribution is a modest increment over simply picking a reasonable constant.

The method has four separate loss-balancing hyperparameters (mu1-mu4) tuned for this specific benchmark setup, and Fig. 6 shows the accuracy is visibly sensitive to their exact values (e.g. mAP degrading as mu1 moves past 50 toward 200) - in the real privacy-constrained streaming deployment the paper is motivated by, it's unclear whether these would need re-tuning for each new domain, and this isn't addressed.

The stated limitations (few-shot new-data stages, noisy new data) are each covered in a single sentence with no experiments quantifying the actual degradation under either condition, despite both being realistic scenarios for the real-world lifelong deployment the paper argues for.
notable: The RFL-ReID vs. traditional L-ReID split is a genuinely useful evaluation design choice: scoring the same trained model under both assumptions (re-indexing allowed vs. not) lets Figure 2's degradation numbers cleanly isolate exactly how much of existing methods' reported performance was implicitly relying on being able to reprocess old raw images, rather than just asserting the problem exists. Also worth noting: unlike several other papers already summarized in this batch, this one's reference list has no obvious duplicate or erroneous citations - a useful data point against assuming that pattern is universal across this literature.
